     IN THE ERCOT REGION                           §                OF TEXAS



          LATE-FILED COMMENTS RESPONDING TO COMMENTS FILED BY
          THE OFFICE OF PUBLIC UTILITY COUNSEL ON AUGUST 11, 2026

        J. Pollock, Incorporated (J. Pollock) appreciates the Comments filed by various parties in

response to the Comments filed by Texas Energy Buyers Alliance (TEBA) on July 30, 2026, and,

specifically, to the study we conducted (TEBA Study). The TEBA Study is the only in-depth

analytical study of an appropriate Minimum Billing Demand (MBD) and obligation period for New

Large Loads (NLLs) in Project No. 58000.1 Among its many findings, the TEBA Study concluded

that a NLL MBD between 75% for 13 years and 80% for 9 years would hold existing customers

harmless. At least 14 other parties submitted Comments which appear to be either generally

aligned with the TEBA Study conclusions, or agree that Staff’s proposed (and OPUC’s supported)

100% for 20 years would be too high a percentage, too long an obligation period, or both.2 In

particular, the Office of Public Counsel (OPUC) raised several issues in its Comments that were

critical of the analysis and findings in the TEBA Study. Because no reply period was established

in this Project, these late-filed Comments are offered to assist in synthesizing the record.

Specifically, we will address concerns raised by OPUC that appear to either misunderstand or

misinterpret the methodology and results of the study. A summary of OPUC’s concerns and our

clarifications is provided in Table 1.

The remainder of these Comments address each individual concern listed above in more detail.

Concern #1: NLLs Would Not Pay For Existing Transmission Investment

       OPUC asserts that the TEBA Study failed to include the costs associated with the existing

network transmission system in determining a MBD percentage and obligation period. As a result,

OPUC recommends that NLLs should pay a higher rate than the TEBA Study indicates. The
 Project No. 58000                                                                   Page 3 of 11
Late-Filed Comments


OPUC Comments state:

       The TEBA analysis focused only on the new incremental transmission costs required
       to interconnect the large load customer with the ERCOT transmission system...The
       costs of this existing transmission infrastructure are not included in the incremental
       transmission costs attributable to large load customers...In actuality, the Wholesale
       Transmission Service or transmission rates that large loads pay should be higher than
       this "breakeven" number calculated as these customers use both the incremental new
       infrastructure and the existing transmission system currently paid for by existing
       customers.3 (footnote omitted)

Contrary to OPUC’s assertions, the TEBA Study recognizes the allocation and recovery of all

network transmission costs attributable to NLLs. The ERCOT Postage Stamp Rate includes the

recovery of all ERCOT-wide transmission costs from all loads, existing and new. We expanded

the Postage Stamp Rate to demonstrate how NLLs would impact ERCOT-wide transmission

rates. The expanded formula is:


                                            Existing TCOS + NLL Incremental TCOS
                ERCOT Postage Stamp Rate=
                                             Existing Customer 12CP + NLL MBD


For example, assume the cost to serve existing customers is $7 billion and those existing

customers place 72 GW of 12CP demand on the system. Further, assume that the incremental

cost to serve NLLs is $4.5 billion and that the NLL MBD is 53 GW. Under these conditions, the

ERCOT Postage Stamp Rate with NLLs would be:


                                          $7 billion + $4.5 billion
           𝐸𝑅𝐶𝑂𝑇 𝑃𝑜𝑠𝑡𝑎𝑔𝑒 𝑆𝑡𝑎𝑚𝑝 𝑅𝑎𝑡𝑒 =                               = $92 𝑝𝑒𝑟 12𝐶𝑃 − 𝑘𝑊
                                              72 GW + 53 GW


And, the ERCOT Postage Stamp Rate without NLLs would be:

                                                 $7 billion
                 𝐸𝑅𝐶𝑂𝑇 𝑃𝑜𝑠𝑡𝑎𝑔𝑒 𝑆𝑡𝑎𝑚𝑝 𝑅𝑎𝑡𝑒 =                 = $97 𝑝𝑒𝑟 12𝐶𝑃 − 𝑘𝑊
                                                  72 GW

As can be seen, both with and without NLLs, all ERCOT-wide transmission costs and loads are

reflected in the Postage Stamp Rate. NLLs would pay the same ERCOT Postage Stamp Rate as


3   OPUC Comments at 22-23, 27.

all other loads because they are providing revenues that will pay for their allocated share of the

ERCOT-wide transmission cost of service (TCOS). In other words, the postage stamp treats NLLs

just like an existing customer being added to the system, except that the MBD is used to ensure

that NLLs provide sufficient revenues to recover incremental costs over a defined obligation

period, even if the contracted load does not fully materialize. An appropriate MBD and obligation

period, thus, prevents cost-shifting.


Concern #2: Any MBD Below 100% Would Shift Cost to Existing Customers

          OPUC also asserts that any MBD below 100% would result in shifting cost from NLLs to

existing customers. Further, OPUC contends that the amount of cost-shifting is directly related to

the MBD percentage. For example, in discussing a hypothetical 300 MW load, OPUC asserts

that a load operating at 90% of its capacity means that only 90% of the cost would be paid by the

large load. Further, the NLL payment would decrease under a 75-80% MBD such that existing

customers are paying the remaining 20-25% of the cost. Specifically, OPUC asserts:

        If the large load usually operates at 90% capacity (270MW compared to 300MW), it is
        assumed that during the 12CP intervals, the large load customer is only using 270MW
        of demand. Thus, the large load customer's allocated transmission costs would be $1.8
        million, instead of the full $2 million costs created to interconnect and serve the
        customer at 300MW…This potential cost shift only increases with the use of the 75%
        or 80% MBD levels… Instead, the large load customer would realize the benefit of
        shifting 20% to 25% of its incremental costs onto residents, small commercial
        consumers, and other ratepayers. Thus, under TEBA' s analysis for a 75% or 80%
        MBD, residents, small commercial consumers, and other ratepayers would pay for their
        share of transmission costs and 20% to 25% of the large load's share.4

OPUC’s assertion that the MBD percentage matches cost recovery percentage reveals

fundamental misconceptions of the function and purpose of a MBD.

          A fixed MBD percentage (whether 100%, 75%, or any other percentage) simply means

that each NLL will have a minimum billing demand, which is the product of the NLL’s contract

demand and the MBD percentage. The transmission charges are then derived from the minimum


4   Id. at 26-27.
 Project No. 58000                                                                        Page 5 of 11
Late-Filed Comments


billing demand. For example, a 500 MW load subject to a 100% MBD and a TCRF rate of $6.00

per kW ($6,000 per MW) would pay $3.0 million per month (500 x 100% x 6,000). Importantly,

this result is only the NLL revenues – it provides no information about the allocated transmission

investment costs to serve the NLL. In other words, the MBD determines the minimum amount of

revenue to be collected from a NLL and not the costs caused by the NLL customer.

         The only way to know whether or not 100% MBD (or any other percentage) generates

enough revenue from NLLs to cover the transmission costs associated with NLLs is to separately

calculate and compare the revenue with the allocated cost. This is precisely what the TEBA Study

does.

         First, Regional Planning Group submissions by utilities that included cost and load

amounts were compiled. Second, revenue at various MBD percentages were compared to the

cost in order to determine the MBD percentage at which NLL revenue would be sufficient to

prevent shifting NLL transmission cost to existing customers. The comparison demonstrates that

a 75% MBD over 13 years or an 80% MBD over 9 years would hold existing customers harmless.


Concern #3: A MBD Obligation Period Should Recover All NLL Transmission Investment

         Another issue that OPUC raises is that any MBD obligation period which does not fully

recover 100% of the transmission investments during the obligation period risks shifting costs to

existing customers. In particular, OPUC proposes 40 to 50-year obligation periods or accelerated

cost recovery from NLLs as follows:

        The MBD should be extended to a longer time period that more closely aligns with the
        useful life of transmission assets, which generally range from 40 to 50 years…Using a
        shortened or reduced MBD time frame increases transmission investment costs caused
        by large load customers that will ultimately shift to residential, small commercial, and
        other consumers. If the Commission elects to adopt an MBD period of fewer than 20
        years, the Commission should incorporate accelerated depreciation into the large load
        cost recovery framework. Requiring large loads to pay a greater portion of their
        transmission-related costs during the earlier years of service reduces the risk that their
        share of costs is shifted to residential and small commercial customers and other
 Project No. 58000                                                                      Page 6 of 11
Late-Filed Comments


        ratepayers, especially if the large load breaks the contract, ceases operations or goes
        bankrupt prior to the end of the 20-year contract period.5

OPUC’s concern appears to address potential tail-end risk; that is, whether any cost-shifting would

occur due to early termination of service. However, OPUC’s proposal to extend the MBD period

(or accelerate cost recovery) is an attempt to use the wrong tool to address tail-end risk.

          The MBD is designed to protect existing customers from paying higher transmission rates

solely because the NLL fails to operate at demand levels sufficient to recover the higher cost of

the investments made to serve NLLs. As previously explained, the MBD, coupled with a defined

obligation period, will ensure that NLLs fully pay for incremental transmission costs. Once the

incremental costs are fully recovered from NLLs, there is no longer any reason to impose a more

stringent MBD obligation on NLLs than applies to existing customers. Further, as discussed below

in connection with Concern #4, applying a MBD beyond incremental cost recovery is both

unnecessary and potentially discriminatory. Thus, it is the wrong tool to address tail-end risk.

          Further, there are better and more effective tools to address tail-end risk. For example, a

contractually required advance termination notice backed up by enforceable security could be

explored. Often, the advance termination notice requirements are rolling (i.e. keep automatically

extending for some period past the initial MBD obligation period) and have notice timeframes

consistent with transmission system planning. Regardless, OPUC’s proposal would take MBD

and use it for the wrong purpose, much like using a crescent wrench to hammer in a nail.


Concern #4: NLLs Should Pay Their Full Share of Transmission Cost in Year One

          In discussing the 75% MBD for 13 years proposed in the TEBA Study, OPUC states that

NLLs should be pay their full [cost] share in the first year. Specifically:

        Consequently, large load customers should be treated equally as other ratepayers
        where in year one, they are paying for their full share of the annual incremental
        transmission costs created to interconnect them, plus the existing bulk system they are
        using for transmission service.6

5   Id. at 5.
6   Id. at 25.
 Project No. 58000                                                                    Page 7 of 11
Late-Filed Comments


OPUC misunderstands the purpose of a single fixed-percentage MBD, which is designed to

ensure that incremental costs are recovered over the entire obligation period and not in any

specific year.

        To illustrate the flaw in OPUC’s reasoning, Chart 1 presents the result of applying 100%

MBD over 20 years, as proposed by Staff and supported by OPUC. The incremental cost break-

even point is depicted by the solid horizontal black line at zero, the annual present value (PV)

revenues are depicted by the dashed blue line, and the cumulative PV revenues are depicted by

the solid red line.




As can be seen in Chart 1, revenues start slightly above the break-even line indicating an over-

recovery in Year 1 (i.e., both the solid red line and dashed blue line are slightly above the solid

black line). This demonstrates that Year 1 costs would be fully recovered under 100% MBD as

OPUC recommends (Year 1 costs are above zero). However, applying this same fixed 100%

MBD obligation over 20 years would result in a ballooning cost over-recovery (i.e. the solid red
 Project No. 58000                                                                    Page 8 of 11
Late-Filed Comments


line’s upward trajectory demonstrates an increasing cumulative over-recovery). By Year 5, the

cumulative PV of the over-recovery is $1.5 billion, and by Year 20 the cumulative PV cost over-

recovery would be $13.1 billion (solid red line). To put this in perspective, the 2026 TCOS for all

of ERCOT is only $6.1 billion.7 Thus, imposing a 100% MBD obligation over 20 years (or longer)

would severely over-collect incremental costs, indicating a MBD obligation that is disconnected

from cost-causation principles and potentially discriminatory.

       By contrast, as illustrated in the TEBA Study, a single fixed MBD of between 75% to 80%,

applied over a defined obligation period, will recover the incremental costs caused by NLLs, hold

existing customers harmless, and avoid a severe over-recovery divorced from cost-causation.


Concern #5: Study Analysis Does Not Reflect Actual Timing of Costs and Loads

       The TEBA Study assumed that NLLs were energized simultaneously with the rate-

effective date of the associated network transmission facilities.       OPUC asserts that this

assumption does not reflect, in OPUC’s opinion, the phased development of how transmission

and loads will be added in actual practice. OPUC then raises the concern that timing mismatches

could be introduced in actual practice that are not considered in the TEBA Study. Specifically:

     The TEBA analysis appears to assume that all transmission facilities and large loads
     will come online simultaneously and that utilities will immediately begin recovering
     transmission costs once facilities enter service. Neither assumption reflects how
     transmission planning, large load development, and regulatory cost recovery occur in
     practice…These timing mismatches create a risk that transmission costs incurred to
     serve anticipated large load growth may initially be recovered from other customers
     until the load fully materializes.8

       OPUC’s primary concern appears to be that if new transmission facilities are placed in

service and recovered in rates before NLLs are energized, it could result in higher rates for

existing customers unless a higher percentage MBD were implemented. Notably, OPUC does



7 Commission Staff's Petition to Set 2026 Wholesale Transmission Service Charges for the Electric
Reliability Council of Texas, Inc., Docket No. 59080, Commission Staff's Final Transmission Charge
Matrices, Attachment A at 2 (Mar. 16, 2026).
8 OPUC Comments at 23.
 Project No. 58000                                                                    Page 9 of 11
Late-Filed Comments


not explain how a MBD obligation addresses what is clearly a timing issue.

       The impact of new transmission facilities will depend on how quickly they are developed,

constructed and placed in service, and how soon the expected loads can be interconnected and

energized. It will also depend on when the costs and loads are reflected in rates. All of these

timing issues are within the purview of this Commission through ratemaking practices that

determine how and when new transmission facilities are reflected in rates and costs are recovered

from customers. None of these timing issues would be improved or degraded by a MBD.

        Further, timing issues are unlikely to be a major concern if history repeats itself. For

example, planning for the CREZ facilities commenced around 2006, physical construction began

around 2010, and the facilities were placed in service around 2013-2014. Transmission build

horizons have not changed appreciably since CREZ. By contrast, NLLs, primarily data centers,

are characterized by aggressive construction and ramp schedules of 2-3 years, which is why

many NLLs are building their own generation and want to interconnect as soon as transmission

service is available. Thus, the most likely scenario, based on history and the characteristics of

NLLs, is that NLLs will start service soon after transmission is available, limiting the risk that

transmission will be reflected in rates before NLLs go into service.

       If the Commission wants to address OPUC’s timing concerns, it need not focus on a higher

MBD. It can instead require TSPs to defer NLL-driven transmission investment to a regulatory

asset until the associated NLLs are in service. This would keep those investments out of rates

until the NLLs are contributing revenues and thereby limit temporal cross-subsidization by existing

customers.


Concern #6: Oncor Is Not A Good Proxy for Residential TCRF Bill Impacts

       OPUC disputes the TEBA Study’s use of Oncor TCRF rates as a proxy for potential

residential bill impacts. OPUC asserts that it is a poor choice because most of the transmission

projects used in the TEBA Study are outside of Oncor’s service territory and its TCRF rate is lower
 Project No. 58000                                                                        Page 10 of 11
Late-Filed Comments


than those of other utilities. OPUC states:

        Lastly, the TEBA analysis applies the Oncor Electric Delivery Company (Oncor) TCRF
        rate, even though a significant portion of the expected $37 billion in Regional Planning
        Group (RPG) projects used are located outside Oncor's service territory. Moreover,
        Oncor's TCRF rate is lower than those of the other IOUs, making it an unrepresentative
        proxy for ERCOT-wide transmission cost recovery. As a result, relying solely on the
        Oncor rate may understate the potential costs associated with serving large loads and
        the resulting impact on residents.9

First, it is important to note that Oncor is the largest utility in Texas and has one of the most (if not

the most) diverse customer base of any utility in Texas because its territory spans major urban

centers, large rural areas, and multiple geographies. Second, the service territory of transmission

projects does not affect transmission rates because all transmission goes into the ERCOT

Postage Stamp Rates that are uniformly applied to all utilities in ERCOT. Finally, because all

customers pay Postage Stamp Rates, transmission rates for utilities may differ temporally, but

ultimately move together. As an illustration, the same analysis in the TEBA Study of Oncor TCRF

residential bill impacts was applied to AEP. Table 2 presents a comparison of the results between

Oncor and AEP.

                                               Table 2
                             2035 Projected Residential Transmission
                                         Billing Reduction
                                (Dollars per Year of Bill Reduction)
                                                 Oncor             AEP
                             Baseline             $0.00           $0.00
                             70% MBD              $3.29           $2.96
                             75% MBD             -$7.26           -$6.53
                             80% MBD            -$17.36          -$15.61
                             100% MBD           -$53.78          -$48.35

As can be seen, both AEP and Oncor move in the same direction with similar residential bill

reductions. The slightly smaller reductions for AEP are likely a result of regulatory lag timing

issues between current TCOS and TCRF rates, which will correct as additional filings are made.


9   Id. at 24.
 Project No. 58000                                                               Page 11 of 11
Late-Filed Comments


In other words, all utilities will ultimately move in the same direction as ERCOT Postage Stamp

Rates, as long as the Commission continues to ensure policies and procedures stay aligned

between wholesale and retail rates.


Conclusion

       We appreciate the opportunity to provide further clarification regarding the TEBA Study

which was filed on July 30, 2026. We continue to believe that a NLL MBD between 75% for 13

years and 80% for 9 years would hold existing customers harmless.

 IN THE ERCOT REGION                            §                   OF TEXAS



 TEXAS ENERGY BUYERS ALLIANCE INTRODUCTION TO EXPERT COMMENT
                       OF J. POLLOCK, INC.

Chairman and Commissioners:

       The Texas Energy Buyers Alliance ("TEBA") respectfully submits the attached expert

comments prepared by J. Pollock, Inc. ("JPI") in Project No. 58000. These comments

supplement TEBA's July 30th, 2026 and August 11th, 2026 filings and respond to issues raised by

parties regarding the TEBA-JPI Transmission Cost of Service ("TCOS") study. The attached

expert comments are intended to provide additional context and clarification regarding the

appropriate design of a Minimum Billing Demand ("MBD") framework for new large loads in

ERCOT.

       TEBA commissioned JPI because the Commission's decisions in this proceeding will

have significant implications for how transmission costs associated with large load growth are

allocated among new and existing customers. As stakeholders have debated appropriate MBD

levels and obligation periods, several different assumptions have emerged regarding how

transmission costs are recovered, what an MBD is intended to accomplish, and what customer

protections are necessary to ensure existing customers are held harmless. TEBA believes it is

important for the Commission to have a transparent, analytical examination of those issues

grounded in ERCOT's transmission cost allocation framework.
        The attached comments focus on a number of areas where TEBA believes the role and

operation of a MBD may have been misunderstood. In particular, the comments explain that an

MBD is a revenue assurance mechanism designed to ensure new large loads contribute sufficient

transmission revenues during the period when incremental transmission investments associated

with their growth could otherwise increase costs for existing customers. The comments further

explain that a MBD is not intended to function as a mechanism to recover all transmission

investment costs over the life of an asset, nor is it a tool designed to address every potential risk

associated with large load development.

       The expert comments also address a central misconception that has emerged in this

proceeding: that any MBD below 100 percent necessarily results in cost shifting to existing

customers. As JPI explains, the percentage value of a MBD alone does not determine whether

transmission costs are fully recovered. Rather, the relevant question is whether the revenues

generated under a particular MBD and obligation period are sufficient to offset the incremental

transmission costs associated with new large load growth. The TEBA-JPI study directly

evaluated that relationship and concluded that an MBD between 75 percent for 13 years and 80

percent for 9 years would hold existing customers harmless. The attached comments provide

additional explanation supporting that conclusion and clarify why a 100 percent MBD should not

be treated as a proxy for cost causation or cost recovery.

       The comments also provide important context regarding the distinction between

transmission costs that are recovered through ERCOT's postage-stamp methodology and the

incremental costs associated with new large load growth. Because all customers contribute to the

ERCOT transmission system through a common transmission rate structure, it is important that

MBD policies align with established cost-allocation principles and avoid outcomes that would

result in over-collection or cross-subsidization.
 Finally, the included expert comments explain that concerns regarding timing mismatches, early

customer departures, or other forms of tail-end risk are legitimate policy considerations, but they

are separate issues that may be better addressed through other tools, such as contractual

commitments, notice requirements, or financial assurances. TEBA believes it is important that the

Commission clearly distinguish between the purpose of an MBD and other policy mechanisms

intended to address different risks.


       TEBA appreciates the thoughtful review that stakeholders have devoted to the TEBA-JPI

study. We offer these additional expert comments to assist the Commission in developing an MBD

framework that protects existing customers, aligns with cost-causation principles, and supports

continued investment and economic growth in Texas.




                                                            Respectfully submitted,

                                                            /s/ Dawn James

                                                            Dawn James
                                                            Executive Director
                                                            Texas Energy Buyers Alliance

Concern #2: Anv MBD Below 100% Would Shift Cost to Existing Customers

        OPUC also asserts that any MBD below 100% would result in shifting cost from NLLs to

existing customers. Further, OPUC contends that the amount of cost-shifting is directly related to

the MBD percentage. For example, in discussing a hypothetical 300 MW load, OPUC asserts

that a load operating at 90% of its capacity means that only 90% of the cost would be paid by the

large load. Further, the NLL payment would decrease under a 75-80% MBD such that existing

customers are paying the remaining 20-25% of the cost. Specifically, OPUC asserts:

      If the large load usually operates at 90% capacity (270MW compared to 300MW), it is

      of demand. Thus, the large load customer's allocated transmission costs would be $1.8
      million, instead of the full $2 million costs created to interconnect and serve the
      customer at 300MW... This potential cost shift only increases with the use of the 75%
      or 80% MBD levels... Instead, the large load customer would realize the benefit of
      shifting 20% to 25% of its incremental costs onto residents, small commercial
      consumers, and other ratepayers. Thus, under TEBA' s analysis for a 75% or 80%
      MBD, residents, small commercial consumers, and other ratepayers would pay for their
      share of transmission costs and 20% to 25% of the large load's share.4

OPUC's assertion that the MBD percentage matches cost recovery percentage reveals

fundamental misconceptions of the function and purpose of a MBD.

        A fixed MBD percentage (whether 100%, 75%, or any other percentage) simply means

that each NLL will have a minimum billing demand, which is the product of the NLL's contract

demand and the MBD percentage. The transmission charges are then derived from the minimum

billing demand. For example, a 500 MW load subject to a 100% MBD and a TCRF rate of $6.00

per kW ($6,000 per MW) would pay $3.0 million per month (500 x 100% x 6,000). Importantly,

this result is only the NLL revenues - it provides no information about the allocated transmission

investment costs to serve the NLL. In other words, the MBD determines the minimum amount of

revenue to be collected from a NLL and not the costs caused by the NLL customer.

         The only way to know whether or not 100% M BD (or any other percentage) generates

enough revenue from NLLs to cover the transmission costs associated with NLLs is to separately

calculate and compare the revenue with the allocated cost. This is precisely what the TEBA Study

does.
          First, Regional Planning Group submissions by utilities that included cost and load

amounts were compiled. Second, revenue at various M BD percentages were compared to the

cost in order to determine the MBD percentage at which NLL revenue would be sufficient to

prevent shifting NLL transmission cost to existing customers. The comparison demonstrates that

a 75% MBD over 13 years or an 80% MBD over 9 years would hold existing customers harmless.

OPUC's concern appears to address potential tail-end risk; that is, whether any cost-shifting would

occur due to early termination of service. However, OPUC's proposal to extend the MBD period

(or accelerate cost recovery) is an attempt to use the wrong tool to address tail-end risk.

        The MBD is designed to protect existing customers from paying higher transmission rates

solely because the NLL fails to operate at demand levels sufficient to recover the higher cost of

the investments made to serve NLLs. As previously explained, the MBD, coupled with a defined

obligation period, will ensure that NLLs fully pay for incremental transmission costs. Once the

incremental costs are fully recovered from NLLs, there is no longer any reason to impose a more

stringent MBD obligation on NLLs than applies to existing customers. Further, as discussed below

in connection with Concern #4, applying a MBD beyond incremental cost recovery is both

unnecessary and potentially discriminatory. Thus, it is the wrong tool to address tail-end risk.

        Further, there are better and more effective tools to address tail-end risk. For example, a

contractually required advance termination notice backed up by enforceable security could be

explored. Often, the advance termination notice requirements are rolling (i.e. keep automatically

extending for some period past the initial MBD obligation period) and have notice timeframes

consistent with transmission system planning. Regardless, OPUC's proposal would take MBD

and use it for the wrong purpose, much like using a crescent wrench to hammer in a nail.

       The impact of new transmission facilities will depend on how quickly they are developed,

constructed and placed in service, and how soon the expected loads can be interconnected and

energized. It will also depend on when the costs and loads are reflected in rates. All of these

timing issues are within the purview of this Commission through ratemaking practices that

determine how and when new transmission facilities are reflected in rates and costs are recovered

from customers. None of these timing issues would be improved or degraded by a MBD.

         Further, timing issues are unlikely to be a major concern if history repeats itself. For

example, planning for the CREZ facilities commenced around 2006, physical construction began

around 2010, and the facilities were placed in service around 2013-2014. Transmission build

horizons have not changed appreciably since CREZ. By contrast, NLLs, primarily data centers,

are characterized by aggressive construction and ramp schedules of 2-3 years, which is why

many NLLs are building their own generation and want to interconnect as soon as transmission

service is available. Thus, the most likely scenario, based on history and the characteristics of

NLLs, is that NLLs will start service soon after transmission is available, limiting the risk that

transmission will be reflected in rates before NLLs go into service.

       I f the Commission wants to address OPUC's timing concerns, it need not focus on a higher

MBD. It can instead require TSPs to defer NLL-driven transmission investment to a regulatory

asset until the associated NLLs are in service. This would keep those investments out of rates

until the NLLs are contributing revenues and thereby limit temporal cross-subsidization by existing

customers.
